title: What to do when your VEP expires in Singapore
excerpt: A photo of my car taken at Seletar Airport According to Singapore Land Transport Authority (LTA), foreign vehicles can only be in Singapore for a maximum of 14…
html:
A photo of my car taken at Seletar Airport

According to Singapore Land Transport Authority (LTA), foreign vehicles can only be in Singapore for a maximum of 14 days. If any longer, you will need to renew it by setting an appointment at LTA's Customer Service Centre in person. 

LTA also states that Enforcement action, including the seizure of vehicles, will be taken against vehicles with expired Vehicle Entry Permit (VEP)s in Singapore. So take note!
This is a story of how I (technically my car) overstayed in Singapore, and it is possible to happen to you too.

TL;DR;

If your vehicle has overstayed more than 14 days (or is about to):

  1. Don't panic
  2. Call LTA Hotline to check for the latest instructions (who knows they may have upgraded to an online application system)
  3. Go to the border checkpoint, insert your AutoPass Card at the immigration gantry, it will alert saying you have overstayed, please visit LTA office. 
  4. Go to the LTA office (it's actually a small counter facing outside)
  5. Present your AutoPass and explain why you overstayed
  6. Pay the fine, pay your toll and daily VEP fees if any, additional charges pay with credit card
  7. Exit Singapore

So how did this happen? 

I was in Singapore to spend Christmas and my birthday with my wife as she works there. We entered Singapore on the 15th of December (Day 1) and happily headed back to our home to rest. Days go by and we suddenly got Covid smack on Christmas! I initially planned to head back the day after Christmas (Day 12), but with Covid, i was stumped and we quarantined at home. 

Knowing about the VEP period, I was checking around what do I need to do. I can't leave my quarantine and drive back to KL (was also very mind fogged and lethargic at that time), nor can i just drive through the causeway and turn back in, it will be so tiring and dangerous for other road users around me. 
I then checked LTA website, which as mentioned above, asks me to set an appointment in person, which also means, I need to wait till I recover and then renew my VEP? Covid can't clear in 2 days and it clearly states that the renewal must happen before the expiry. So, I still went to try and make an appointment. Lo and behold, the next available appointments are in January (the next week about 8 days from Christmas).
So, I called LTA with 1800-CALL LTA (1800-2255 582). The lady on the line just said, "Pay the fine". Wait, what?  How much is it? 
1000 SGD. 
Wow, so there are no other option for me to renew my VEP? Well, how do I do it? 
She said there's a counter after the immigration booth. I asked where? 
And she couldn't explain where or how it looks like.
So fine, I stayed on until I got better, and then headed off for KL. By then, it was already Day 19. I nervously headed to Tuas Checkpoint preparing to vomit out 1k SGD, and when I got there, the first thing I asked the immigration officer was, "Where is the LTA office? I overstayed my VEP". 
He replied, "Oh really ah? just park your car at the side and the office is just on the side". 
He returned my passport then I went for the nearest car park, which have only 2 car parks.

Now where is the LTA office? I was looking for a door but right next to the car park are just toilets. I walked around, and started to worry if i was considered wandering around the checkpoint too long, would they get suspicious? I walked all the way to the customs lane and that was already the exit. There was no clear indication and i tried pushing some doors, but the office rooms there were abandoned. I walked back towards immigration and thats only when I found the LTA office (from the position i stood to take photo of my car at the car park, it was just on the right of me), it was actually just a counter on the wall, not an office.

I went up and spoke to a young gentlemen there. I declared that I overstayed, as I got Covid and couldn't get an appointment, and the lady on the LTA hotline just told me to pay the fine. I had no other options to renew my VEP. He then made a phone call, probably to HQ for some advice. Once he put the phone down, he said sorry, you will still need to pay the fine. 
My heart sank. There goes 1,000 SGD. I tried to plea and say that there was no other legal option for me to avoid this situation. 
He then adds, "You will still have to pay the fine first, then you can email LTA to appeal".
Oh well, then he asks, "I will deduct a rounded off from your AutoPass, the rest will be over credit card?"
I said yes, that's typically the process anyway. 
"Ok, i will deduct 350 SGD from your AutoPass and 100 SGD on credit card", he says.
Confused, I asked if that is without the penalty. He then says the total includes the penalty. 
"How much is the penalty? How much is the fine for an expired VEP, or overstaying my VEP" 
"10 SGD", he says.
Wow what a relief. I told him that I was informed it was 1000 SGD, and he said no. He mentioned that the fine was only 10SGD, but if you still prolong your stay, it could increase. So far, I cannot find any table or information on how much the fines are for exceeding the VEP period. 
So how to avoid this from happening? If you plan to stay longer than 14 days in Singapore with your car, set an appointment with LTA for a date close to the expiry to apply for a renewal. Other than that, usually by 14 days and if you drive regularly, you will need to pump petrol anyway so it is a good reason to go to Johor to pump petrol, and come back into Singapore, which will also reset the VEP days.

title: The Dangers of Formaldehyde and You May Already Be Living With It
excerpt: As any home owner, we love to look for the best and high quality cabinets when we plan to stay there. The first thing in my mind was, it has to look good and…
html:
As any home owner, we love to look for the best and high quality cabinets when we plan to stay there. The first thing in my mind was, it has to look good and follow the theme that I want. For me, the living area were Muji style and the bedroom and kitchen were Modern Dark. 


In KL, I managed to find a very good interior designer who was able to execute my wishes and customisations very well. The choices of materials were good and high quality, and the final product looks good. However, I overlooked one most important thing.

What is Formaldehyde? 

Formaldehyde, which is a colorless, strong-smelling, flammable chemical that is produced industrially and used in building materials such as particleboard, plywood, and other pressed-wood products. In addition, it is commonly used as a fungicide, germicide, and disinfectant, and as a preservative in mortuaries and medical laboratories.  

When I first moved into my home, I noticed that when I open my cabinets, my throat will start to burn and my eyes will start to sting and get very teary. It was not until then I only learned about Formaldehyde which is used as a adhesive and coating for wood. It was so bad that I could not pack anything into my cabinets and searched on the internet on how to solve it, and this is what I had to do.

How to get rid of Formaldehyde?

I had to ventilate my unit. I live in a condo and I am lucky to have balconies and a rear open yard which i can open them fully and get natural wind channeling through my unit. This also welcomed dust and insects from the outside. On top of that, I have a Coway Lombok III air purifier, and electric dehumidifiers in all rooms. All cabinets were left open and I have not filled them up yet. I did this for a month and started moving in my stuff, but the sting and burns were still there for at least another 5 months, not till a year that I wasn't bothered by it anymore. 

This problem has also surfaced on the news in Singapore, where kids were falling sick from this problem: https://www.channelnewsasia.com/singapore/formaldehyde-wooden-furniture-homeowners-seeking-help-sick-4475181 . This is a serious problem even for adults. While we know the short term effects are instant burns in the eyes and throat upon inhalation, it could actually cause cancer in the long run based on this study, where Formaldehyde can cause nasal cancer in rats.

How to avoid exposure to Formaldehyde? 

So how can we keep ourselves and family safe from these unseeable dangers? Firstly, look for renovators, cabinets, furniture and wardrobes that have certifications and ratings of safe Formaldehyde usage. There are different standards depending on region but Malaysia follows Europe and China ratings, which are as follows:

  • E2 Grade >0.124mg/m³

  • E1 Grade ≤0.124mg/m³
  • E0 Grade ≤0.050mg/m³
  • Super E0 (SE0/SEO) ≤0.030mg/m³ —> Malaysian Only Standard
  • ENF Grade ≤0.025mg/m³ equivalent to USA CARB-NAF at 0.04-0.06ppm (0.0536mg/m³-0.08mg/m³)

Does Malaysia care about ratings and certifications? Basically no, in the Bolehland of Malaysia, anything is possible. But one thing for sure, ZBOM Manufacturing is certified ENF and E0 along with Global Green Tag. Have you checked the likes of Signature Home, The MakeoverGuys, Kubiq etc?
But wait, ZBOM Malaysia has ENF and E0 international certifications? What is ZBOM? How do they have such high certifications? 


What is ZBOM?

Well, ZBOM is a wardrobe and kitchen cabinet producer who has 5 Mega Factories over a cumulative span of 5 Million SqFt that operates autonomously using the intelligent manufacturing system of German HOMAG.
Quality is made from precision, and with precision we get consistency, and with consistency, we achieve safety standards. ZBOM manufacturing has a list of these certifications:
  • Global Green Tag
  • China Environmental Label Certification
  • FSC International Forest Certification
  • SGS System Certification
  • CFCC - China Forest Certification Council
  • CGP - China Green Product
  • China Environmental Labelling
  • CARB NAF - not listed / equivalent to ENF
  • EPA NAF
That's a mouthful right? But premium quality products will get its foundations right first in its manufacturing process to make sure its produce are as good as the producers. But certifications aside, this is my personal take of experiencing ZBOM products. 
I visited ZBOM Malaysia Showroom in Sunway Velocity, Cheras while it was still under renovation and the cabinets have already arrived on site. The first thing that really surprised me was, there was no formaldehyde sting or burns at all, besides the dust from cement. And once they have opened their doors a month later, there was still no signs of formaldehyde burns and stings, and they could operate right away.


So the most important factor in determining a good quality cabinet has been checked, formaldehyde rating. How about its finishing, durability, water resistance? With over 10 different materials to choose from, each have their own purposes and capabilities along with the style you have in mind. 

But it doesn't just stop there. ZBOM has an array of accessories that will help with your storage solutions as well!

title: Canon RF 35mm f1.8 Macro IS STM Review
excerpt: Pros: Great travel lens Small, compact and lightweight Great aperture at f/1.8 Macro capabilities Cons: No weather sealing No dedicated focus ring No clicks on…
html:
Pros: 

  • Great travel lens
  • Small, compact and lightweight
  • Great aperture at f/1.8
  • Macro capabilities
Cons:
  • No weather sealing
  • No dedicated focus ring
  • No clicks on the RF control ring
  • No setting to define focus range (macro - infinity)
  • Autofocus can throw off to Macro searching for subject
The 35mm lens is the first of 2 RF mount lenses at this focal length, one at f1.8 (Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 Macro IS STM) and the other as an L lens at f/1.4 (Canon RF 35mm F1.4 L VCM). This review is only for the f/1.8 version. 


I have been having this lens now for a year and I bought it from Georges Cameras in Sydney, great service from them and I always get my gear from them when I'm there. Best part is as a foreigner, I get tax refund so the prices are sometimes cheaper than at home in Malaysia. Why a 35mm? 

35mm was a street standard and you would find lots of vintage cameras including mountable lenses and rangefinders to be 35mm in focal length. This has become a common street lens standard for many, giving a view that has less distortion but wide enough to enjoy. 


However my sentiment with the lens after few months of usage was about the opposite. I find the 35mm lens to be not wide enough for landscapes, nor not zoomed enough for portraits. Since then, this lens has sat in my dry box for a very long time. The only time i use it is if I am travelling and i want a low light lens at f/1.8.


For work, I also barely uses this lens but its on standby as a back up in my camera case. Most of the time i will use zoom lenses for it's versatility, as i shoot events mainly which I still practice the holy trinity:
  • Canon EF 16-35mm f2.8 L iii USM
  • Canon RF 24-105 f2.8 L IS USM Z
  • Canon EF 70-200 f2.8 L ii IS USM
With these 3 lenses, i never needed to use prime lenses. The only exception, is when I have a closed setup and when I take products close up. This lens is amazing for static automotive photography. 






This lens excels in taking close up or detailed shots of car parts, or any product parts if needed. 

Is the Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 lens good for videos? Well, yes and no. 


The RF 35mm fits well on a Canon R8 on a DJI Mini 3, which is a compact camera gimbal great for traveling. One day in Sydney, i was able to take cinematic shots of a car meet with just this setup (start from 1:39)

The only annoying thing about this RF 35mm f/1.8 is that when it tries to focus, it will go through the whole range from macro to infinity, searching for a subject especially when it's low light. This focus throw is very slow and there is no way to stop it from searching slowly but to wait till it reaches macro, and then it tries to zoom out to infinity again. 
There are 2 types of lens hoods that you can get for this lens, a circular hood or a flower petal type from JJC. After buying the petal lens hood, I find it quite fiddly and hard to naturally attach it on and off as it is quite tight. 

So again, is the 35mm a great travel lens? If you like simplicity and light weight, definitely. I'm abit different. I love compression and shots that are more than 100mm. In my last post, I talked about how I ditched the RF 35mm for the Canon RF 24-240mm, and now I use the RF 24-240mm 90% of the time for travelling. The RF 35mm remains as a backup lens for night use, but even with that, I still have been shooting car shots at night with the 24-240mm on a tripod.

title: Canon RF 24-240mm f4-6.3 IS USM Review
excerpt: Pros: Exceptional travel lens Very versatile zoom range (10x) medium weight at 750g acceptable sharpness acceptable bokeh ( compared to a 24-105 f4-7.1 IS STM…
html:
Pros: 

  • Exceptional travel lens
  • Very versatile zoom range (10x)
  • medium weight at 750g
  • acceptable sharpness 
  • acceptable bokeh (compared to a 24-105 f4-7.1 IS STM)
Cons:
  • No weather sealing
  • Dark aperture range at the telephoto end (but not a problem! read below)
  • No dedicated focus ring
  • No clicks on the RF control ring
  • extending zoom barrel
Now just because there are more cons listed, doesn't mean it's a bad lens. Now let me tell you a story. 
This lens was on my list for awhile. I recently travelled to Tibet, Nepal and Bhutan with the Canon EF 16-35mm f2.8 L iii and the Canon EF 70-300 f4-5.6 L, both are exceptional lens but at a cost, of price as well as weight. During hikes, i often had to swap lenses because i love to take landscapes and, i love to get compressed street photography. 

A photo I actually shot of me having to change lenses in the middle of the hike up Tiger's Nest, Bhutan

Throughout this trip, i constantly was yearning for a 24-240 lens. Canon RF had it since mid 2019 and it wasn't actually till this year (2024) that i realised this lens existed, mostly because I am more focused on the L lens lineup of Canon. When I found out about the 24-240, I was excited and skeptical. As usual, would an entry lens perform as well as the L variants, and at the price of about almost MYR 4,000, I could almost get the RF 24-105 f4 L which I had before and i knew it wasn't enough because i love compression shots at about 200-300mm. 
So, I couldn't decide and told myself, I shall challenge myself to take travel photos with just a 35mm, as I have the RF 35mm f1.8 Macro and its great!
2 weeks later, I had a trip to Hong Kong and i stuck to my promise, "don't spend more, the 35mm is enough" and happily packed a small bag with just my Canon R8 and that 35mm prime. First night in Hong Kong, I was already enjoying the night street shots already. 

Hong Kong 7 eleven shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 @f/1.8, 1/125, iso 250


Hong Kong bus commuter at a bus stop shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 @f/1.8, 1/125, iso 320


Locals crossing the street in Hong Kong shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 @f/1.8, 1/125, iso 320

That night, all was well, not until i arrived at Macau the next day. 
I have been so busy lately trying to start up my biz and technically restart my Photography career, that I had no time to research about where I am travelling to. I usually take it in as a surprise and adventure, and this is where i really got surprised.

Hotel Grand Lisboa, Macau shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 @f/4, 1/2500, iso 200
I didn't know this hotel, that is gold in color, and been famous on Instagram for quite some time, is actually in Macau. It is called the Grand Lisboa, I always thought it was at some other place in China, but the moment I saw it, I instantly regretted. I need my 200mm! Well i was able to capture it in a 35mm frame but, it wasn't enough! I seen before that there was a street that could get a good compressed shot and capture its magnificence. 
So walking on around Macau, in my head I just cant stop thinking and finding where can I buy this lens, here right now. Even at the Ruins of St Paul's Cathedral, I could see Grand Lisboa and I'm like, wow what a shot this will be if i had a telephoto. 

All I could get with 35mm of Grand Lisboa shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 35mm f/1.8 @f/8, 1/640, iso 200

I even tried to use my iPhone 15 Pro which had only up to 3x optical zoom. I got the frame but it wasn't satisfying. 
Shot on iPhone

So we had some extra time and I began hunting for camera stores. Initially I arrived at Nice Digital Company, and it was out of stock. I was thinking, this lens must be good enough that theres no stock and I rarely see it on the 2nd hand market. Ok one last try, we walked to Maxim's Photo Supplies, and they had stock! So the listed price was abit expensive, but the uncle there was nice, he gave me a price i could get as cash locally in Malaysia. So there it was, I straight away took it and put it on my camera. 

The Canon R8 paired with the Canon RF 24-240mm f4-6.3 IS USM

I also got a UV filter straight away because I don't want to regret like how my other lenses got scratched on the lens element, just breaks my heart. 
And straight away, I went to hunt for the shot of Grand Lisboa parallel to the streets, and here it is!

Hotel Grand Lisboa, Macau shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/250, iso 200, 70 mm


Hotel Grand Lisboa, Macau shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/640, iso 200, 157 mm

As you can see, even the wide angle shot was already at 70mm, and we could go in way closer to get more detail of the hotel at 150+ mm. Now, let me show you what it would have looked like at 35mm.

Hotel Grand Lisboa, Macau shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/200, iso 200, 35 mm

Pretty boring isn't it? I was so satisfied after getting this lens, and now comes the question, was it worth it? How does the lens perform in low light? 

Staircase of Hong Kong MTR Station shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/4, 1/125, iso 2500, 24 mm


Streets of Hong Kong shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/100, iso 12800, 198 mm

Both scenarios at both ends of the minimum aperture stops shows an acceptable performance of low light capabilities. To me, in photography, the thought process is like this. Composition and shutter speed is more important than noise or grain. You can fix a noisy photo but you can't fix a motion-blurred photo. Although sharpness may be lost, it is still crucial to capture the moment. 
So, focal length and low light capabilities checked, how about its bokeh? 

Portrait in a cafe shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/125, iso 2500, 123 mm


The Hustler in the rain shot with Canon R8 with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/80, iso 12800, 157 mm

What do you think? Not bad isin't it especially against the RF 24-105 f4-7.1.
So, does this lens' capability just ends here? No. This lens is also a capable motorsports lens!
Recently I was shooting for Motul Awesome Racing Team for Sepang 1000km Endurance Race. I was focusing on video using the Canon RF 24-105mm f2.8 L Z and the Canon EF 70-200mm f2.8 L ii, but I had my Canon RP with the RF 24-240 as a backup and for some photos. Here are the results!

Motul Awesome Racing Car 511 shot with Canon RP with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/80, iso 800, 183 mm

Motul Awesome Racing Car 511 night shot with Canon RP with Canon RF 24-240mm f/4-6.3 IS USM @f/6.3, 1/100, iso 3200, 129 mm

Despite the noise rendered for the night shot, its highlights are sharp and clear and I can say this lens is motorsports ready! The only challenge (or benefit) is that this lens is lighter than regular telephoto lenses, so depending on how you shoot your pan shots, heavier lenses tend to be more stable. 

Conclusion

This lens at its price point may be one that you would look away from, but once trying it out and hearing from many other users, they vouch for this lens and I have become one myself too. It will be more suitable to be used outdoor and if you have indoor events, its still better to have a fixed f/2.8 lens or a prime lens. Ultimately, this is a very good lens for travelling where i dont need to carry and switch around multiple lenses to get a wide and zoomed shot.

title: Canon RF 24-105 f2.8 vs f4 vs f4-7.1
excerpt: In the full frame landscape, the 24-105mm range has been the most versatile yet limiting lens to professional photographers. They have about 4 stops of zoom…
html:
In the full frame landscape, the 24-105mm range has been the most versatile yet limiting lens to professional photographers. They have about 4 stops of zoom ratio but usually have a fixed aperture of f4 which wasn't acceptable to wedding photographers and rather not good enough for indoor shoots. Most professional shooters go for the steeper 24-70mm f2.8 lenses which is part of the holy trinity of lenses, or if not, the sharp and fast prime lenses. 

But then again, these lenses still exist for a reason. The 24-105mm f4 lenses from various brands got its name as a kit lens as it did come with some full frame camera combos, but has existed for very long and adopted by 3rd party lens makers. I myself have been a big fan of the 24-105 f4 lenses because im mainly a landscape and travel photographer. 

I initially fell in love with this lens when I was using the Sigma 24-105 f4 DG OS HSM Art on my Canon EOS 6D Mk ii. This was a wonderful combination as I could get wide angle and some compressed shots. The Art series from Sigma is also tack sharp. Although being almost half the price and arguably sharper to its Canon L competitor, it actually was way heavier and bigger.

But enough about my history and love of 24-105mm lenses, lets get to the meat of this topic!


At this point of time, the current 24-105mm lineup of the Canon RF series are:

- Canon RF 24-105mm f2.8 L IS USM Z

- Canon RF 24-105mm f4 L IS USM

- Canon RF 24-105mm f4-7.1 IS STM

One of them is exceptionally expensive, that you could buy 10x of the third lens for the first one! But lets dive into them one by one.

Canon RF 24-105mm f4-7.1 IS STM

Pros:
  • Super light at 395g
  • Smallest of its lineup
  • Cheap at about RM 1,500 (Shopee)*
  • Overall sharp
  • Fast Autofocus
Cons:
  • Bad aperture range (would have been nice if the minimum aperture could max out at f5.6)
  • no weather sealing
  • Hard to create compression or depth of field
Good for:
  • Travelling
  • To be used at high risk places
Bad for:
  • hired shoots
  • night photography
So im not gonna go all technical, im just gonna share my experience and sample shots. 
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM 60mm f5.6 1/500 iso 100
This was taken at the Kek Lok Si Temple on Penang Island on a bright afternoon. Its worth mentioning that a CPL filter was attached which makes the sky much more blue. We can see that the image is sharp for f5.6, and its something that is acceptable to capture memories or for travelling, but how about when it gets darker?
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM 24.0 mm f8 1/80 iso 6400
Here we can see that there is much softening of the image due to higher iso. It is still acceptable for something that goes into the family album, but i wouldnt recommend for editorial. As mentioned, it is hard for this lens to create depth or bokeh due to its minimum f7.1 aperture at its full zoom length of 105mm.

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM 105 mm f7.1 1/80 iso 320
The pillars in the foreground are still clear and identifiable whereas the statues remain to be sharp. In the image below, the temple in focus is way further than the previous image, and the buddha in the foreground is still clear. 

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM 24 mm f4.5 1/500 iso 100

In terms of landscapes, it does keep everything in detail and sharp. 

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4-7.1 IS STM 60 mm f5.6 1/500 iso 100

Personal sentiment and verdict - Honestly the shots were disappointing, especially when depth could not be established. Its weak low light performance wouldn't outshine a modern hand phone today. The reason why i took this out for a trip is because its too costly and heavy to bring out the RF 24-105 f2.8 L for a road trip. If you have some budget, i recommend upgrading to the RF 24-105 f4 L, which i will be talking about next, or try the RF 35mm f1.8 Macro IS STM.

Canon RF 24-105mm f4 L IS USM


Pros:
  • It's an L lens 
  • Cheapest Canon RF L lens at about RM 4,700 (Shopee)*
  • Very sharp throughout
  • Weather sealing
  • Fast Autofocus
Cons:
  • Weighs about 700g
  • More depth only at the further zoom ranges
Good for:
  • Travelling
  • Outdoor event shoots
  • Motorsports
Bad for:
  • night photography
I honestly miss this lens, because it just fits into the bag for an all in one setup. The only drawback i had with it was shooting at night and indoor events where ISO had to be bumped up quite high. An f2.8 aperture makes a big difference compared to f4 for indoor shoots and im the type that avoids using speedlights. 
But this lens was easy, i could take it along with me for morning drives and it will take stunning automotive shots. 

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4 L IS USM 47 mm f4 1/200 iso 400


Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4 L IS USM 91 mm f4 1/200 iso 250

In terms of bokeh, there is a fair amount of background separation especially around the 105mm range.

Canon EOS RP RF24-105mm F4 L IS USM 105 mm f4 1/500 iso 12,800


Canon EOS RP RF24-105mm F4 L IS USM 105 mm f4 1/500 iso 200

When paired with a speedlight for studio product shoots, it is sharp throughout and makes clean shots. 
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F4 L IS USM 45 mm f8 1/80 iso 400

Personal sentiment and verdict - The f4 variant is great and capable, but when doing hired jobs, it may not cut it when dealing with low light situations or if you want to get very shallow depth. Prime lenses are great for this but in the rush of the moment, the lack of zoom could affect your framing, composition or story telling. This is where the RF 24-70 f2.8 L IS USM is well known for. 

Canon RF 24-105mm f2.8 L IS USM Z


Pros:
  • It's an L lens (again)
  • Very sharp throughout
  • f2.8 aperture giving better background separation
  • very light and smooth zoom ring
  • Weather sealing
  • Fast Autofocus
  • new features like the iris aperture control and power zoom which requires a separate device (also denotes the Z part of the lens name)
  • Very hybrid design for both video and photo shooting
  • 2 extra function buttons which i honestly never used
Cons:
  • Very expensive at about RM 14,599 (Shopee)*
  • Weighs about 1.3 kg
  • Not fully removable tripod ring (Only the tripod attachment slides off leaving a mount)
Good for:
  • Professional shoots and events
  • Video Production
  • Borderline good for portraits
  • Motorsports
  • Automotive
Bad for:
  • traveling
Ok so the biggest question everyone has about this lens is, how does it perform in portraits?! Honestly i'd say, dont expect much for an f2.8, but see for yourself:
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/4000 iso 400
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/640 iso 200
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/640 iso 100

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/640 iso 160

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/1250 iso 100

They're not too bad isin't it? Whats important is the background separation that is enough to put focus on the subject and still get to tell a clearer story. Now lets have a look at some events. 
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 43 mm f2.8 1/500 iso 100

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/125 iso 1000

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 24 mm f2.8 1/250 iso 1250

The thing about RF lenses is that it's so sharp, minimal choma, has good contrast and vibrance. Well, how about low light conditions? 
Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 27 mm f2.8 1/125 iso 4000

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 25 mm f2.8 1/160 iso 8000

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 64 mm f2.8 1/125 iso 2500

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 105 mm f2.8 1/160 iso 2500

Canon EOS R8 RF24-105mm F2.8 L IS USM Z 63 mm f2.8 1/100 iso 640
In these shots, no flash has been used and fully dependent on the lighting provided. The f2.8 really makes a difference for low light situations. 
Personal sentiment and verdict - The lens although feels good, has nice ergonomics, balanced weight and renders amazing photos, its not something that i would want to bring out just for fun. 
The lens is huge that it doesnt fit many of my bags. I always have to unmount it to be able to transport it around. Carrying an expensive lens is also worrying, and becomes a liability. I find myself looking for alternatives when i pack my bag for trips (which is where i borrowed the 24-105 f4-7.1 lens).
This lens is no doubt production ready, and is for serious business. You can store this in a case and bring it out only when you have a paid gig, thats how i would characterise this lens. 
The ringing alternative in my head will be to sell this and go for a 24-70 + 70-200 setup, but (again) having that extra 70-105 mm in a lens is really a trade off that is hard to let go because you do lose time when swapping or switching lenses than to just have that further reach when needed. 

End Notes

I hope this comparison has helped you in choosing which of these lenses you should go for. Basically, these are the 3 characters for each lens:

Canon RF 24-105mm f4-7.1 IS STM - youre new to photography, still figuring out the technicalities, want something light and in a budget

Canon RF 24-105mm f4 L IS USM - you been shooting awhile, but you are a hobbyist, maybe get paid once in awhile or never stressed over clients

Canon RF 24-105mm f2.8 L IS USM Z - youre serious about nailing every shot and can never miss a moment, must be able to shoot indoors and outdoors, and zoom into the moment when needed. huge budget but believe a few jobs can pay off the lens.


*I am not associated with these stores, link is for reference on the current market

title: How does the Canon RF 24-105mm f2.8 L IS USM Z lens perform and known issues
excerpt: 24-105 lenses has always been known to be versatile, multi purpose and sometimes being so underrated that its dubbed as a kit-lens. That's not the case for me…
html:
24-105 lenses has always been known to be versatile, multi purpose and sometimes being so underrated that its dubbed as a kit-lens. That's not the case for me as an avid traveller, where i have been using 24-105 lenses from the Sigma Art 24-105mm f4 DG OS HSM to the Canon RF 24-105 f4 L IS USM. 

When I started to do more professional work indoors, the f4 did hit a limitation for low light shots, bumping ISO on my Canon RP up to 12,800 which still gave acceptable results, but not enough for professional readiness. 

The Announcement

Then, the 24-105 f2.8 was announced! It was crazy and revolutionary from Canon (IMO), because no one has made such a fixed aperture lens ever yet. I really love how canon is going on their lens ranges, which are understandably expensive. The RF lenses from entry level up to L rings are tack sharp. One of my primary lenses for videography is the Canon RF 35mm f1.8 Macro IS STM which is small, great for gimbal and can be very close to subject. 


So back to the 24-105 lenses. The f2.8 version is still very new and we have no idea when will we get ours in Malaysia. Speaking to my trusty supply from KLDSLR, Adrian estimated it would arrive in mid February. So in the end oddly, I went to get the Canon RF 15-35mm f2.8 L lens instead. 

The 15-35 is a great street and indoor range. I only got to use it a few times and I could already feel that it doesn't feel enough for me. Having a 24-70 or 24-105 is a much safer focal length to shoot events. 

Arrival In Malaysia and Price!

One fine day on the 24th of January, i got a text from KLDSLR saying that the lens has arrived, and theyre holding a set for me! I was like, I will be there after lunch! 


The lens is definitely expensive, at about MYR 14,699.00 which you can almost buy 2 L lenses. But this was a target of mine since it was announced, this was my focal length. So I went for it and traded in the 15-35 L to be able to afford this. I'm probably the first in Malaysia to own this lens.

First Impressions

The lens was undoubtedly huge, almost the size of the EF 70-200 f2.8 lens at about 199mm vs the latter at 207mm. The weight tho, was nice. It was very mid heavy but it didnt feel heavy at all. Mounted to my compact Canon EOS R8, it didnt feel unbalanced and I can still shoot with one hand. But more details and visuals on my first impressions in the video below:

Practicality

Last weekend, I got to shoot a graduation ceremony. This has a mix of wide angle family shots, and compressed portrait shots, and some wide portraits with campus backgrounds. This was the perfect lens for the job. Along with it, i had an EF 50mm f1.2L USM mounted to my Canon RP for much shallower portraits. 


Overall, I have used the 24-105 f2.8 for at least 90% of the time. The sharpness and background separation is satisfying enough that i did not feel the need to pull up my 50mm f1.2. 

Canon RF 24-105 f2.8 L IS USM Z @105mm f2.8

Canon RF 24-105 f2.8 L IS USM Z @73mm f2.8

Comparing to the 50mm f1.2

Of course we cant compare a prime to a zoom lens, but I wanted to compare the lens to the shallowest depth of field I have to show how much depth does the 24-105 f2.8 have. 



From theory we know that the f2.8 cant give as much depth and softness as to a f1.2, but it is acceptable in being able to highlight the subject to be in focus.

Videography

The zoom ring has almost no restrictions making it easy to rotate, not to mention it only takes a quarter of a turn (90 degrees) to zoom from 24mm to 105mm. While being handheld, i can easily "power zoom" with my fingers smoothly. 


I tried mounting this lens with my Canon R8 on a DJI RS3 mini gimbal and dont bother trying. the weight distribution which is located closer to the lens mount position is hard to achieve, unless you have an external rig to set the plates in balance, but will definitely add more weight to the gimbal. So this lens is a 100% handheld setup for me at this moment. 

Known Issues

Update: Lightroom Lens correction has been fixed with v2! and it works perfectly fine now


Previously:
While I was editing my photos in Lightroom, I noticed that the edges were digitally stretched. Confused at first, I went to see if this was an image or camera problem. My RAW photos didnt produce that issue so I narrowed it down to Lightroom. True enough, the lens corrections from Lightroom has a bug where the digital stretching are artificial or there is just no data. 

This problem only occurs when Lens Corrections are turned on. Initially I thought i could solve it by turning all of them off, but that is not the case. You still will need lens corrections at around 24mm wide as it has strong vignetting. 
without lens correction

after lens correction
This means you have to individually check your images one by one if there are any affected and adjust them accordingly. 
More details are explained in my video below:
This issue is also being discussed on this Adobe Community thread.

Overall

I am very pleased with this lens for its IQ and versatility. The size of it (weight is not an issue) and price is what puts me off from this lens. I hope that it will be practical in the long run, as we will only find out after doing rounds and rounds of gigs and see if we can keep up with it.

title: Lufi XF Mapping for Subaru CVT, how to do it yourself!
excerpt: The latest update of the Lufi XF has allowed it to read Subaru CVT Transmission Fluid Temperature. You may have the mapping already in your device, or you can…
html:
The latest update of the Lufi XF has allowed it to read Subaru CVT Transmission Fluid Temperature. You may have the mapping already in your device, or you can copy the file manually into your device. 

Firstly, head into the main menu and look for User Data Setup (9).



Choose any of the PID 1 - 9 that is available to add your mapping.



Under File Location, go to USERPID <DIR> -> Subaru <DIR>.


Here, there are 3 ATOILT files and you need to trial and error which file works with your car model. 

Try the first ATOILT1.INI by selecting it, and hold the middle button to go back.


Go down to Request Test If it says Time Out, then you need to try again with ATOILT2 or ATOILT3. If all of them Time Out, unfortunately the mapping does not work with your vehicle. 


But if you get a response, means you have found the correct mapping.

You can leave the other values to default. 


Set your display to support the new mapped value, and you will be ready!


This has been tested with:

  • Lufi XF on Subaru WRX (S4) VAG and Levorg VM
  • Lufi XS on Subaru WRX

Info thanks to Eric Foong.

title: All you need to know about Puspakom B5 and B7
excerpt: This article is written to share my personal experience in going through a Puspakom inspection. A Puspakom inspection is required if you are transferring…
html:
This article is written to share my personal experience in going through a Puspakom inspection. A Puspakom inspection is required if you are transferring ownership or selling your vehicle.

It is important to know that if your vehicle is still under loan or hire purchase, both B5 and B7 inspection are required, whereas if the car is fully paid, only a B5 is required.

TL;DR:

  1. Make a booking for one / both inspections at https://www.mypuspakom.com.my/
  2. Bring your Vehicle Grant, MyKad and Booking QR 
  3. Go to the inspection centre
  4. Show Booking QR to guard, follow instructions on which lane to go
  5. Register at counter providing Vehicle Grant, MyKad and Booking QR
  6. Hand over your vehicle at the lane (you cannot be in the inspection area so go to the waiting room)
  7. Wait for your car number plate to be called out (or check the status on TV screen depending on the centre)
  8. Take the report and your Vehicle Grant back

What is B5 and B7?

A B5 inspection is called Ownership Transfer (Tukar Milik) a.k.a 9014 and a B7 inspection is Hire Purchase (Sewa Beli) a.k.a 9812.

The table below shows the items inspected from each report:

B5 B7
Engine Number
Chassis Number
Marks of joints and weld
Window Tinting
  • Opacity/Transparency
  • Installation (Neat/Bad)
N/A Number Plate Condition
N/A Exhaust Silencer and Size
N/A Engine Mounting
N/A Flooring
N/A Wheelhouse Condition (under fender cover)
N/A Body Condition
N/A Window Condition
N/A Tyre Condition and Thread
N/A Pillar Condition
N/A Odometer Reading
N/A Chassis Frame Condition
N/A Air Conditioning Tempreature
N/A Gear Box Condition
N/A Type of Fuel
N/A Suspension and Axle Play
N/A Side Slip Rating
N/A Brake %
N/A Smoke Emission
N/A Headlight Angle


To clarify, everything under B5 will fall under a B7 report but you still need to book both.

Why did I do it myself?

Most people actually assign runners to do this because it does take time (one hour for me). What I heard is that these runners can charge between RM 100 — RM 400 per inspection.

Do note that the cost of Puspakom inspections for B5 and B7 are just RM 30 and RM 60 respectively (If you have done a booking on Puspakom official website, there may be an additional booking fee). Also take note that if you fail any inspection, you will need to redo them with the same charges.

Notice that you could be paying RM 300+ extra to get this inspection done. But runners are convenient, it’s your choice. Just remember that some car insurances doesn’t cover all drivers.

What do you need / Preparation?

  1. Original grant or Pink Slip or Vehicle's Registration Card (Original) / Vehicle Ownership Certificate (VOC)
  2. Your IC (MyKad)
  3. Your booking QR code (there is a walk in option but usually B7 will need booking)
  4. Your vehicle (It is advised to remove any stickers on windows, as well as tinting on the front 3 windows as mine failed, and keep all personal belongings and valuables with you)

Example of a Vehicle Grant

Getting Started

Make a booking by visiting https://www.mypuspakom.com.my/. Create an account if you dont have one.

Click on Branch Reservation on the top left.

Fill in the form accordingly.

Choose the type of inspection accordingly. Tick on Tukar Milik for B5 and Sewa Beli for B7.

Choose the inspection centre of your choice, and date. Take note of the color codes that represent the availability. You can only choose the Green and Yellow boxes.

Choose your time slot.

Choose Representative or Owner. Review your application and then continue the process until its complete (I have already done my inspection so I cannot demonstrate that here).

If everything was successful, you should be receiving an email of your booking which will look like below.

Arriving At The Inspection Center

Rule of thumb, if you see a line of lorries, thats not for you.

When arriving, show your QR invitation at the guard house. They will inform which lane is for you.

Cheras Inspection Centre

Seremban Inspection centre

You will be in line with the rest of the cars that are undergoing inspection. At the end of the first queue, you will need to register at the counter with your IC, Vehicle Grant and Invitation QR.

Queue in Cheras


Queue in Seremban

After registration, you will be led to the inspection lane. At this point, the inspector will take over you car and you will have to wait at the visitor lounge. Leave the vehicle grant with the inspector.

The left lane (Mazda) is just for B5 and the right lane (Proton) is for B7 in Cheras

The B5 test will only check you engine and chassis number, joints and welds, and tinting.

The B5 lane is very simple

The B7 inspection will be more thorough. Puspakom has a diagram to explain it.

Once the inspection is complete, your car will show its results on a TV, or a representative will say out your car plate number. They will hand over your report and vehicle grant. Below are the examples of a B5 and B7 report:

Sample of a failed B5 report due to window tinting

Sample of a B5 report that has passed

Sample of a B7 report that has passed

Apparently I have failed my B5 report due to window tinting. The shop that installed it claimed to be within JPJ regulation. However, the original glass of the vehicle already has some opacity. take a look at these 2 readings.

The report on the right is the window visibility of the original windows without tint. There is already a 20% loss of transparency on windows. So it will be a good idea to remove the tint before heading into inspection. This only affects the front windscreen and the front side windows.

Once you have your report, dont forget to collect back your Vehicle Grant, and you’re done.

Side Notes

The inspection centres can be very noisy and messy. I am grateful to be assisted by the lorry uncles and brothers who have guided and explained to me on the processes and report. Hopefully this guide will give you a clear view on the expectations, so that your process will be much smoother.

title: How to Upgrade Your Car Radio into a Smart TV for Cheap
excerpt: I wanted to upgrade the head unit of my car without having to spend hundreds and waste the original one that is still working. I suddenly had the thought to…
html:
I wanted to upgrade the head unit of my car without having to spend hundreds and waste the original one that is still working. I suddenly had the thought to use a TV stick and plug it into the car radio.

So before we get too excited, we need to acknowledge that this only works with a car radio or head unit that have a screen and HDMI inputs. You need to be familiar on how to access to your car radio. If you are not, you can follow my guide here for a Subaru Forester SJ 2018. The methodology should be similar which is to always use plastic tools and if it doesn't come off, it probably needs to be unscrewed. 

Prerequisites:

  1. XiaoMi Mi TV Stick Android TV with ChromeCast
  2. HDMI Extender (1m) (optional but recommended to easily change HDMI accessories)
  3. Plastic tools - to open the dashboard safely
  4. Screwdrivers - to open the head unit

HDMI access is usually behind the radio / head unit

Once you know you have a HDMI input available, you can now get a XiaoMi Mi TV Stick Android TV with ChromeCast. You will also need a usb power source to charge the stick. 


Before starting,  I would recommend you to plug the TV stick into another monitor or TV first to set it up (android first startup process). The process can take awhile and may be uncomfortable to do it from the car directly. 

Once you have all the tools ready, open up your dashboard to access to your car radio. Refer here for a dashboard opening guide. 

Remove any existing HDMI attachments to it. If you have a HDMI extender, plug this into your car radio. 

Run the HDMI extender towards your glove box. This means you will be able to remove the TV stick anytime from the glove box and not having to open your dashboard again. 

Powering your TV stick - check if your radio has an existing usb input. This can be used to plug the micro usb cable to charge the TV stick. Be mindful that if you are using this for USB audio, you may want to consider another way to charge the TV stick, such as a USB cigarette lighter charger. Run your Micro USB charger to the glove box as well. 


Before closing up your dashboard, test the device connection to the radio. Turn on the radio and set to HDMI. Make sure the TV Stick is also charging. It will boot up automatically upon receiving power. Test it with Spotify or Netflix.

Once everything is done, do some nice wire management and close back your dashboard, and enjoy the ride. 


FAQ

  1. Is this touch capable?
    - unfortunately no, everything works only from the remote. 
  2. Does it need WIFI?
    - yes, you need to provide it internet. The easiest way is to connect to your mobile phone hotspot. 
  3. There are some existing cabling for the HDMI on my radio already. Can I remove it? 
    - Yes you can. This is usually attached to your screen mirroring device provided by the manufacturer. Rule of thumb, dont cut any wires so you can put them back. 
  4. Will doing this void my warranty? 
    - yes it could, so do this on your own discretion. Much safer to not cut any wires and dont break any of the warranty stickers.
  5. When my car is moving, the display is blank. But it shows when my car is parked. Why?
    - Some cars have a safety system where it only allows videos to be played when the car is stationary. There is a wire that is either attached to the speed or the gears of the car. If you really want to bypass this, please go to a professional car electrician. Again, this is based on your own discretion, and always drive safely without distraction. 
  6. My radio only has a USB port. Can I use this device? 
    - Unfortunately no, it needs a HDMI input to feed the audio and visuals.
  7. Can i use a USB to HDMI converter?
    - also no, you need usb to power the TV stick and the HDMI to feed the AV.
  8. Can this work with a headrest monitor?
    - it depends on your headrest monitor, it needs to have HDMI input and has to be powered by micro USB. 
  9. How did you connect this to your OBD?
    - I connected using a WIFI OBD device, which also means that there will be no internet. I wouldnt recommend it anyway because you cant touch the screen and most OBD apps wont work with the remote alone.
  10. Have you tried installing android auto?
    - no, i didnt want to custom flash my TV stick
  11. Have you tried using navigation apps?
    - yes i did and it didnt work well. Waze screen remains blank, and you need the touch screen for them to work. Also its a pain to type in the search with the remote. The device has no GPS as well.

title: 2006 Perodua Myvi | Cleaning Spare Tyre Compartment
excerpt: The ice box in my trunk spilled water into the trunk and I'm like, shit! What am I gonna do? After a simple look into the lower compartment of the trunk, I…
html:
The ice box in my trunk spilled water into the trunk and I'm like, shit! What am I gonna do?

After a simple look into the lower compartment of the trunk, I found the drainage plugs below the jack holder. Knowing that I can flush the trunk, I decided to give it a good clean as it's filled with grease and asphalt. Here's how to do it.


Remove everything from the trunk, that includes the spare tyre, the emergency triangle, the jack etc.


Look for the drainage plugs. It looks something like the picture above.



Use a flat head screw driver to lift the plug off.

Start washing. You can use your car detergent or a normal kitchen detergent with an old sponge. After washing, do wipe the trunk with a dry cloth to make it easier to dry. Be careful with wiring in the car. Some cars may have wiring for license plate or tail lights or even speakers or your 6 disc CD changer. Try not to wet electrical sensitive items or your cushions.


Ta-daa! All cleaned up. Leave the car under the sun to dry. Make sure it is really dry before installing drain plugs and placing back the items into the trunk. Having water retained in the trunk may cause metal tools to rust.

Do comment if you have any questions or if you'd like to correct me or share your experience.

Cheers.

title: VR Box | Adding the Magnetic Switch
excerpt: The VR Box is a wonderful mobile VR headset that is comfortable and sturdy to be used. However, it lacks the magnetic switch that makes it difficult to…
html:
The VR Box is a wonderful mobile VR headset that is comfortable and sturdy to be used. However, it lacks the magnetic switch that makes it difficult to interact in certain mobile apps including Google Cardboard app. With that, I modified my cardboard to have a magnetic switch. What was needed was, a Google Cardboard v1 or a replica of it that has the magnetic switch. It is important to know that Google Cardboard v1 only has the magnetic switch and the v2 doesn't as it is replaced by a touch button to support more mobile devices.


I started by removing the front panel of the VR Box. You need to remove the phone holder to do this.




Then, we remove the front panel. This can be done by lifting its clips off upwards from the inside with your thumb.


Once the inner part is exposed, unscrew the 4 screws on each corner.



After that, place the magnet inside as following. Make sure the magnet is still strong enough to hold the second magnet on the outer side. When comfortable with its position, use a hot glue gun to stick the inner magnet in place. Do not glue the magnet on the outer side as it is suppose to move. I also salvaged the cardboard piece to mount the magnet in place.


When the inner magnet is finally in place, screw back the inner panel and clip back the front panel. Rest the outer magnet on the side of the VR Box. We need to know the position of the magnets so we can nicely glue the outer cardboard in place to keep the magnet in the groove. Once confirmed, we can glue the cardboard onto the VR Box.


Ta-daa! Looks abit ugly but its functional. Feel free to paint the cardboard black so it blends with the headset.


Do comment if you have any questions or if you'd like to correct me or share your experience.

Cheers.

title: 2006 Perodua Myvi | Change Fog Lamp
excerpt: As a first post for this blog, I'll be just doing a little intro on what this blog is all about. I love to DIY, but it's difficult in Malaysia in many ways…
html:
As a first post for this blog, I'll be just doing a little intro on what this blog is all about. I love to DIY, but it's difficult in Malaysia in many ways, including the difficulty of getting desired parts and tools that are not cheap here. Secondly, Malaysian products rarely have DIY guides. Thus, I am documenting this, from my experience as it may differ to anyone else, to probably help that very small population of people who do self maintenance towards their products.
I own a 2006 Perodua Myvi, it's the very first generation of the car if im not mistaken. Over time, the headlamps and fog lamps tend to turn yellow due to the sunlight's UV rays but it cleans off well over a polish. However, my fog lamps were cracked and smoked so I decided to get them replaced. 
Changing the fog lamps for this car is quite easy. You just need a flathead screw driver to pry the lamp off the bumper. Insert the screwdriver from the edge of the lamp that is closer to the center of the car.


Once the lamp clips off the bumper, you can just pull the lamp off.




Unclip the wire from the bulb. The socket has a lock so just press it to unclip.


A brief introduction to the lamp, the red circles are the bumper clips that keeps it in place. The blue joint is the alignment adjuster. This helps angle the fog lamps up and down. The bulb is L-shaped, tightly placed in the center with rubber washers built onto the bulb. This prevents water from going in. If you want to remove or replace the bulb, twist it anti-clockwise and pull it out.



To put the bulb back into the lamp, you can push it in and twist it clockwise. Make sure all the three pins are properly place and twisted into place so that it will be tight and aligned. You may place back the fog lamp if you are just replacing the bulb. If you are replacing the whole lamp, the following steps are the same but with the new lamp.


Just like removing the wire socket from the bulb, clip it back on. Rest the lamp on the bumper and test whether the light works.

To place the lamp back into the bumper, simply lay the lamp into place gently, then push the outer edge of the lamp first (the edge closer to the sides of the car) with some force until it clips in. That is the adjustment joint clipping into the bumper. Only after you clipped in the adjustment joint, the rest of the lamp can be clipped in by gently forcing the lamp into the bumper. It should fit in place.

If you have more time, you can align the lights according to your liking. You just have to repeatedly remove the lamps and adjust the length of the adjustment joint until both the lamps are angled the same.

Issues:
The lamp was Malaysian made and bought at about RM55 per piece. Usually the Taiwan versions are better but cost almost twice as more. There are also other Malaysian made lamps but the price ranges between RM55 to RM75 per piece. Being the cheapest, one of the lamps could not clip in properly. This is due to the lamp not being made properly, or that my bumper couldn't clip it properly. However, the old lamp clips in properly. I had to use some rubber gum to tighten the clip in place. Nevertheless. the lamp shouldn't fall off as long as the adjustment joint is clipped into place. It has been 2 weeks of driving, clocked about 600+ km through sunny days and heavy rains and its still in place.

Besides that, sometimes the adjustment joints clips in too tight. You can just pull the lamp off even harder but make sure that your bumper is held sturdy. The clip will be stuck on the bumper after, but can be removed with a screwdriver as it unclips when pinched.

Do comment if you have any questions or if you'd like to correct me or share your experience.

Cheers.

title: Video | Creating a Budget Music Video
excerpt: Being all inspired to make videos with my new Canon EOS 60D has got me hyped up to make a video before my semester break ends. At times, I will day dream…
html:
Being all inspired to make videos with my new Canon EOS 60D has got me hyped up to make a video before my semester break ends. At times, I will day dream stories in my head about the videos I can produce. It’s easy to imagine stories, but it’s hard to write scripts and to record the video itself.


I won’t say that I have professional equipment but I know it’s sufficient. In this post, I’m just going to talk about how I made my MV just to share my thoughts and knowledge with you. My equipment line up was simple.

  1. Canon EOS 60D
  2. Canon EF-S 18-135mm f/3.5-5.6 IS (kit lens)
  3. Canon EF 50mm f/1.8 II (cheapest Canon lens in the market, but awesome)
  4. Tamron 10-24mm f/3.5-4.5 (discount on Amazon.com)
  5. Zoom H1 (cheapest range but great quality by brand)
  6. 160 LED Video Light (cheap light)
  7. A few tripods and gorillapods.



Zoom H1
Samsung Galaxy S2 Metronome Beats
I’ll be honest. This is actually more than enough to make a good video. I’ve seen people out there like Dreambitious, The Salad Show and other college film productions making great videos with just a dSLR and their kit lenses only. But if I have these lenses so, why not use them?
Before making the video, we needed the soundtrack to be the backbone of our video. Aaron a.k.a. A.RON wanted to do a cover by Teddy Geiger, For You I Will. Do note that this video was only made by me and Aaron. I went to Aaron’s house to do the audio recording. We set up the Zoom H1 onto a tripod at the corner of his room and padded its surroundings with pillows and blankets. This was done to prevent echoes from bouncing back on the walls. To prevent any other external sounds, we turned the fan off and also the air conditioner.



All of the sounds were recorded separately. For instance this acoustic cover involved 1 guitar and 1 vocal recorded separately. A pair of headphones was plugged into the Zoom H1 for monitoring purposes. In one ear, Aaron also plugged in another earphone as that was used as a metronome. The metronome was an Android App on my Samsung Galaxy S2 called Metronome Beats. It was used to make sure that his timing was accurate which makes editing and post processing easier.



The earphone was added under the headphone. 

Basically, one instrument must be recorded on perfect timing before another instrument or vocals come in. If you record for a band, the drummer will do his recording first before the other instruments and the vocals will be last. In this case, we recorded Aaron playing the guitar first while guided by the metronome.
For the vocal recording, we used the recording of the guitar instead of the metronome in the earphones. The headphones as usual was for him to monitor himself during the recording. Both recordings were then combined and added with certain sound effects.


On another day after the song was ready, we started shooting our MV. We decided to go to Sunway Pyramid car park roof top to shoot. It was a cloudy day, but dramatic too. We had no script as we just wanted to shoot random scenes. I think this isn’t a good idea as it’s always better to have a script ready. Doing that will save a lot of time. Another tip for creating an MV is to always have a backbone track. A backbone track, in my terms, means to have a full video of that song taken in one take. It doesn’t matter if it’s a still or on a dolly, but just have one video rolling throughout the song. This is a backup plan during post production as sometimes when editing, you will find out that you don’t have enough scenes, you can just take any from the backbone scenes. Backbone scenes also can be used as main scenes, intro and outro too.


Above: Shooting a scene on the roof top
Below: I use Magic Lantern in my 60D

Do check online or magazines to learn good camera angles, rule of thirds or many other tips in filming. A normal advice is to always keep your camera as stable as possible, which I still need to work on a lot. It is advised to use lenses with Image Stabilizers as much as possible. Do take note that post processing is important in making an interesting video. My thought at first was to not apply colour correction at all to my video to keep it natural, but instead I decided to add leave colour and set a cool temperature to my video. It’s all up to you.
This was what I had in my mind while doing and learning from making an MV. I hardly read articles on videos and photography, which is a bad thing, as I prefer to try things on my own and learn from them. If you have any more tips or suggestions to improve my video, do comment below.
Thanks.

download this track at https://www.facebook.com/dadeft/app_178091127385



If you notice, there was a lot of jitters in my video during motion. This was a known irreversible error in the video editor. Fixing it will result in redoing the whole video again. This is one downside of this MV.

title: Music | How to re-string your acoustic guitar step by step..
excerpt: Hey yo! alright.. i know maybe many of you know how to re-string your guitar, but there are many who dont, or dont dare.. So let me give you an advise.. You…
html:
Hey yo! alright.. i know maybe many of you know how to re-string your guitar, but there are many who dont, or dont dare.. So let me give you an advise.. You can cut service charges ($$$) by restringing your guitar on your own, and it would be a good experience too..

Be patient and dont worry if you break your strings, especially if its your first time. During my first time, i was scared like sh*t.. but after awhile, i kind of mastered it.. my restringing and twining has become much neater already.. So i have thought of putting up a post for those who wants to know how..

First, what you need.. (Please read through the whole post first before taking action.. This is to be familiar of the steps and mistakes that may occur.) 

a tuner.. this is important when you tighten your strings.. It keeps you in track if it is too tight or not and prevents your strings from breaking..


Cloth, same as those used to clean glasses.. Sweat from hands will cause rusting on strings.. always clean your strings..

A plier.. used to remove pins from the bridge of the guitar.. 

A set of new strings..

A flat surface.. Usually a table but i do not have a big table so I use my bed..
So, whats the first step? 
(note, DO NOT REMOVE ALL YOUR STRINGS FIRST. you may loosen the tension of the guitar between its neck and body and damages may occur.. DO RE-STRINGING 1 BY 1)
First, know the pattern of your guitar's tuning board.. 

Usually it is a V-shape for an acoustic guitar.. Basically the string run inwards to out..

Then, know the position of strings..

  • 1st string is an e-string.. this is the smallest string in diameter.. its the furthest string at the bottom of you hold a guitar in position.. 
  • 2nd is the b-string..
  • 3rd is the G-string..
  • 4th is the D-string..
  • 5th is the A-string..
  • 6th is the E-string, which is the thickest..
The illustrations shown by me will be the re-stringing of the D-string.. The steps are also applied on the other 5 strings.. 
So, we un-tune the string.. When the string is loose enough, we can just use our hands to unwind the string off.. 
un-tune the string..
The string as it gets looser.. this image shows that im pulling the string off..

String is removed.. 
 Now, at the bridge..
This is the bridge of your guitar.. As you can see, my D-string is loose..

If you can, pull its pin with your fingers.. 

If you cant use your fingers, use a pair of pliers.. I think there is a much more proper tool than this, but lets say we dont have it.. 

Well like I said, use a much proper tool.. The plier may damage your pin like the picture above, but if you do it gently, there is no obvious damage.. my other 5 pins are still looking good even after I used pliers.. (Personal note: this is where I learnt when to use the pliers gently.. So you gain experience from doing.. )

When the pin is removed, this is how it looks like.. remove the old string.. 

To install the new string, place the 'ball' of the new string right below the pin.. 

Push it into the hole..

Pull the string alittle to make sure its tight.. 
Next up, fit in the other end of the string into the tuning board.. 
the hole.. 

insert the string into it..

pull the string as much as you can.. give a space allowance of 5cm to 7cm.. after that, push it back.. this is a space allowance for winding.. 

lock it by making a slight twist, its like a hook.. 
tune back your string..  If winding is too little, the strings may come off the tuning board by itself, but if you wind too much, tuning will be hard.. best is to have about 3-4 rounds.. thats why there is about a 5-7cm allowance.. Do not tighten the strings all the way just yet (important for next step).. 
Fit the strings nicely into the nut, its alike a second bridge but at the neck (image above)..
Red circle: I did not place the string into the nut properly and tuned it.. this is wrong..
Orange circle: the groove for the string to go in..
Green circle: a properly fit string..
use a tuner to keep track of the string's tune or tension.. tuning a guitar too tight off its note may break the string.. always be careful and patient.. 

a clean wind, nicely done.. do not worry about its excess strings all over yet.. it is important in case the winding is not enough..
Repeat the steps for the other strings.. 
Old strings, what to do? Well these strings are still usable unless they are snapped.. Keep all strings in case you snap a new string before a performance and need a spare, lets say.. 
Excess strings, what to do? Alright, these strings are dangerous for the eyes.. These strings are sharp and fine and can cause injury.. use a wire cutter to cut off the excess strings when you are confident with the installation of your strings.. 
take care.. =)
